artists.biography:
Jeffrey Scott "Jeff" Buckley (November 17, 1966 – May 29, 1997), raised as Scott "Scottie" Moorhead, was an American singer-songwriter and guitarist. After a decade as a session guitarist in Los Angeles, Buckley amassed a following in the early 1990s by playing cover songs at venues in Manhattan's East Village, such as Sin-é, gradually focusing more on his own material. After rebuffing much interest from record labels and his father's manager Herb Cohen, he signed with Columbia, recruited a band, and recorded what would be his only studio album, Grace, in 1994. Rolling Stone considers him one of the greatest singers of all time.
Over the following two years, the band toured widely to promote the album, including concerts in the U.S., Europe, Japan, and Australia. In 1996, they stopped touring and made sporadic attempts to record Buckley's second album in New York with Tom Verlaine as producer. In 1997, Buckley moved to Memphis, Tennessee, to resume work on the album, to be titled My Sweetheart the Drunk, recording many four-track demos while also playing weekly solo shows at a local venue. On May 29, 1997, while awaiting the arrival of his band from New York, he drowned during a spontaneous evening swim, fully clothed, in the Mississippi River when he was caught in the wake of a passing boat; his body was found on June 4.
Since his death, there have been many posthumous releases of his material, including a collection of four-track demos and studio recordings for his unfinished second album My Sweetheart the Drunk, expansions of Grace, and the Live at Sin-é EP. Chart success also came posthumously: with his cover of Leonard Cohen's song "Hallelujah" he attained his first No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Digital Songs in March 2008 and reached No. 2 in the UK Singles Chart that December. Buckley and his work remain popular and are regularly featured in "greatest" lists in the music press.

perplexity.description:
Live at Sin-é documents Jeff Buckley's early solo performances at the intimate East Village coffeehouse in New York City, recorded during two nights in July and August 1993. Originally released as a four-track EP in November 1993, the recording captures Buckley in a stripped-down setting—voice and guitar alone—interpreting a mix of original compositions and carefully chosen covers that reveal his eclectic influences. The EP includes "Mojo Pin" and "Eternal Life" (Buckley originals), alongside interpretations of Edith Piaf's "Je N'En Connais Pas La Fin" and Van Morrison's "The Way Young Lovers Do," showcasing his ability to inhabit diverse material with emotional depth and technical precision.

The release marked Buckley's first commercial recording and arrived at a pivotal moment in his career—while he was simultaneously beginning work on his studio debut Grace at Bearsville Studios in Woodstock. Sin-é held particular significance for Buckley as a performance space where he had developed a devoted local following, and the venue's intimate atmosphere allowed him to demonstrate the spontaneity and creative vulnerability that would define his artistic identity. The EP introduced audiences beyond New York to the distinctive qualities that had already impressed regular attendees: his remarkable vocal range, fingerstyle guitar work, and interpretive sensibility drawing from rock, folk, and art song traditions.

The original EP's modest four-track format proved influential enough to warrant expansion; a deluxe Legacy Edition reissue appeared in 2003, packaged with additional material and documentation. While the initial 1993 release operated primarily as a calling card for devoted listeners and industry insiders, it established the template for Buckley's artistic approach—intimate, intellectually engaged, and emotionally unguarded—that would resonate throughout his brief but consequential recording career.
